tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. A call a usage limit refused, or one still running when the run stopped, usually runs again without ending reuse: finished calls after it still come from cache. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Skip it for session upkeep (compaction, boot notes, reading batch results, scheduling agents: coordinator skill, read after this file), Stop hooks, disk or container trouble (cloud-container), other repos, and general Fortress history."
6:# Working in the Fortress revival repository
29:: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.
71:4. Fold each expression of numerals alone into one exact value: a numeral, a quotient of two numerals or a boolean (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").
92:The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).
133:- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`; a numeral coercion's static parameters follow their own rule: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
134:- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion does not change which declaration runs when one already fits. A numeral is the one exception: it can run a more specific declaration that its coercion reaches. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
177:- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
195:- How revived Fortress differs from the team's Fortress and from the languages that you know: `references/revival-changes.md`
204:A task usually needs several parts. Every task needs `records.md`, for its queries and its report. If a task reads or changes the original tree (its Java and Scala, the library, the tests or the specification), or reviews such a change, read `revival-changes.md` whole, after this file, before work. A task that only runs a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a commit does not need it, until it must read a failing test's source: then read it. For example, a fix of walk needs `revival-changes.md`, `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.

component XXXGenericTraitFunctionalMethodsNestedWalk
export Executable

(* Two generic functional methods of a trait with a static parameter, the one over U extends Round inside the one over T extends Shape, are a valid overloading by the Return Type Rule, and a call takes the more specific one that applies; Specification/advanced/overloading.tex, section "Declarations with Static Parameters". *)

trait Shape end
trait Round extends Shape end
object Circle extends Round end
object Square extends Shape end

trait Holds[\S\]
    which[\T extends Shape\](self, x: T): String = "shape"
    which[\U extends Round\](self, x: U): String = "round"
end
object H[\S\]() extends Holds[\S\] end

run(): () = do
    h = H[\ZZ32\]()
    assert(which(h, Circle), "round", "a Circle takes the more specific declaration over U extends Round; overloading.tex, section \"Declarations with Static Parameters\"")
    assert(which(h, Square), "shape", "a Square takes the declaration over T extends Shape, the only one that applies; overloading.tex, section \"Declarations with Static Parameters\"")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

For a generic object that lists `T` first in its `extends` clause, no test covers such a body (row 1052). Before a compiled program relies on one, write a compiled test of it.

+When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). In a departure, the checker also reads the intersection where an object redeclares an abstract dotted method of `T` at the same parameter types (row 1094). There the intersection is the object's own type, so the two declarations have one domain, and the checker accepts them only with the same return type. So it refuses a narrower return type in the object, which the rule accepts and walk runs. Declare the object's method at `T`'s return type, with the object's type for `X`. For a method without parameters, you can declare both methods as getters instead, called as `x.m`, not `x.m()`: the pair then compiles with the narrower type. With the reading of the exclusion test and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. In two cases walk does not read `self` so, and its load check refuses the valid pair (row 999):

+- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.
+
+**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values take a subscript, as `a[i]`: an array, for example. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile.

The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Two departures:
+
+- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
+- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).

+**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. Walk departs for numbers of two run-time types at one position: it refuses them, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Where the deciding elements' own comparison is `Unordered`, the answer is `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.
+
+**Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence, `SEQV` (P-168).** Strict equivalence is the operator `≣` (STRICTLY EQUIVALENT TO), written `SEQV` or `===` in ASCII. The operator `≡` (IDENTICAL TO, `EQV` or `EQUIV`) is a different one: logical equivalence on booleans. The interpreter's library declares it and its negation `≢` (`NEQV`) for booleans only, so on other values each is a type error. The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:
+
+- values of different types are never equivalent;
+- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
+- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
+- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.
+
+So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Two string literals of one text are one object (P-171). So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are `true`. Two string literals joined by `||` fold into one ("Numbers"), so `("a" || "b") SEQV "ab"` is `true`. A float numeral converts where `RR64` is declared ("Numbers"), so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `RR64` 0.5. The interpreter's library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false` (row 923). To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its `≣`, declared as `===` over `Any`, follows `SEQV` but compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).

+## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes
+
+**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: in a generic object whose `T` stayed open, a call `pick((1, 2))` of its methods `pick(x: Any)` and `pick(x: (T,T))` runs the first (row 663). Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
+
+- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
+- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
+- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
+
+**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
+
+**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
+
+- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
+- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
+
+The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension without its condition (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
+
+**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
+
+**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call runs only under walk, also after the switch-over. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, which lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.
+
+## Numbers
+
+**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** In both libraries, seven are value objects (P-178): `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64`. In the interpreter's library, `QQ` is a trait, and its values are the value object `Ratio` (P-166). The compiler's prelude declares no `QQ`. Do not extend a number type in a program. Declare a program's own number type below `Number` (P-160). Such a type runs on both paths. Both paths refuse an object declaration below one of the seven, as `object Mine extends ZZ32`. Walk refuses it at load: 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'. The compiled checker refuses it: 'Invalid type in extends clause: ZZ32'. The record calls the number types "the tower", though they do not nest.
+
+**The team's `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` do not exist.** No library declares them. On both paths, each is undefined as a type: 'Float is undefined.' In their place, write `ZZ32` for `Int`, `ZZ64` for `Long`, `RR64` for `Float`, `ZZ` for `BigNum` and `NN64` for `UnsignedLong`. A `typecase` arm at such a name, or at any name that names no type in scope, gets the same message. Write an arm over every value as `x: Any =>`: the team's `x =>` reads `x` as a type, and is refused. In a tuple arm, an undefined name is still read as a binder that takes any element, on both paths, and no message names it undefined (row 1064). So under walk `(NoSuchType, ZZ32) =>` takes `("s", 3)`. Compiled, with an `Any` selector, the checker refuses that arm: 'The typecase clause, Pattern at ..., is unreachable.'
+
+**A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** A numeral's own type is `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` with a radix point (P-174). Its static arguments are the numeral's numbers: `n` the digit count, `m` the count of digits after the point, `r` the radix, and `v` the digits read as one integer in that radix, so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. Both lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`. No numeral value exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type. The compiler's prelude follows the same design (P-37).
+
+A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs. Walk's message depends on the place: a top-level binding gives 'Type mismatch binding', a parameter 'got arg'. To get an `RR64` infinity, write `import Constants.{infinity}`. Test a value `x` with `x.isInfinite`.
+
+Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value, other than a numeral type's number, is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).
+
+Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A program's own number type takes a numeral through a coercion generic over its numbers, which its body declares, as `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 }`. With a radix point, write `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])`. The static arguments of either form are naturals of any size. In the body, each converts where it stands, into the type that its place fixes. A numeral whose number does not fit there is refused statically. It is a `ZZ` only where nothing fixes a type (P-174, P-173, P-40). So `Byte`'s body is `Byte(v)`. The tree departs: walk, the checker and the code generator read each as a `ZZ`, so walk refuses `Byte(v)` (F-341, F-342, F-347). Under walk, write `Byte(v.asZZ32)`, as the one library does: the getter raises `IntegerOverflow` outside `ZZ32`'s range. The `where` clause bounds the numerals that the type takes. The checker refuses statically a numeral that breaks it, as `300` here: 'The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte.' Walk refuses it when the binding runs. A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches the type as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written: walk computes it at the place's first run, the compiled path when the class loads, before `run()` (`compiler.md`, "What the code generator does"). Each run of that place reuses it (P-176). Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.
+
+**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one exact constant, which converts as a numeral does at one of the eight number types, or takes its default. A quotient that is not whole stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. Except for a negated numeral, as `-3` above, a program's own type takes the constant only through a coercion from its default type, since coercions do not chain (P-174). So `h: Half = 10/20` needs `coerce(q: QQ)`; a numeral coercion is not enough. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
+
+**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). The rule converts at a declared return type too, but walk does not (row 387). Nor does walk convert a function argument from its arrow type to the parameter's, as `inc: ZZ32 -> ZZ32` passed at `f: ZZ32 -> ZZ64`: 'Unification error' (row 1083). Declare the function at the parameter's arrow type. Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". If one of them takes the call's numerals at their default, it runs instead: `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` is `RR64`'s product, not `QQ`'s.
+
+**A numeral can run a more specific declaration than the one that fits its default type (P-46).** On both paths, a call with a numeral runs the declaration that fits the numeral's default type, unless the numeral's coercion reaches another declaration whose declared parameter types are strict subtypes of the first one's. Then the other runs. So `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`, but `f(1.5)` runs `f(x: RR64)` beside `f(x: RR32)`. Two departures:
+
+- under walk, a numeral in a call whose other argument is a variable declared `Any` converts by that value's run-time type, as `a = 0` for `a: Any` (row 1016);
+- on both paths, `g(5)` runs `g[\T\](x: T)` beside `g(x: NN32)`, where the rule gives `g(x: NN32)` (row 1017).
+
+**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
+
+**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types converts into `RR64` by its own getter, `x.asRR64`. The one library departs: each declares `asFloat(self): RR64` instead, so write `asFloat(x)` (F-324). Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has no `asFloat` (`compiler.md`). Generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, this conversion among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. A numeral reaches a number type's own `=` by its coercion (P-46). So on both paths `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true` and `u =/= 0` is `false` for a zero `u: NN32`. Under walk, `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y` for an `RR64` `y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead.
+
+**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
+
+**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with the one library's `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
+
+## Reductions and comprehensions
+
+A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
+
+**Where a reduction's bound names its parameter, as for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, the two paths fix an unwritten static argument from different places.** The argument is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Without it, the checker takes the reduction's expected type, and the body's type only where there is no expected type or it does not fit the reduction's bound. So `x: RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)` sums `ZZ32` elements in `RR64`, not in the body's type. A reduction whose bound does not name its parameter takes its bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types; if it is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1".
+
+At a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable and an assignment, the checker reads the declared type, so the two paths sum in different types (row 1008): `meth(): RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#4] huge(j)` raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk only. Write the argument there in a program for both paths. A call's argument has no expected type where the call is accepted without one. So as a call's argument, a reduction sums in its body's type on both paths. Write both arguments of `BIG MIN_MAX`, the element types of its pairs, as `BIG MIN_MAX[\ZZ32, ZZ32\][j <- 0#3] pr(j)`: the checker infers only a single static parameter (row 1007). Departures under walk:
+
+- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
+- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
+- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
+
+**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one fails at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
+
+## Implementation limits
+
+**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). Besides a `Boolean`, walk takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition.
+
+**Write every parameter type.** The compiled checker refuses a parameter without a type, "Missing parameter type for", unless the exported api's declaration gives the type. Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

## Failures

### 1. C: walk's half of the refusal of a number that does not fit is lost

**Old** (`revival-changes.md:99`): "The tree departs: walk, the checker and the code generator read each as a `ZZ`, so walk refuses `Byte(v)` (F-341, F-342, F-347). Under walk, write `Byte(v.asZZ32)`, as the one library does: the getter raises `IntegerOverflow` outside `ZZ32`'s range."

**New** (`orientation.md:99`): both sentences are deleted. The paragraph keeps only this sentence on a number that does not fit: "In the body, each converts where it stands, into the type that its place fixes. A numeral whose number does not fit there is refused statically."

**Source** (F-407): "Walk binds each as a static number whose default is a `ZZ` …, which converts where its place fixes a type as a folded constant does and is refused there when the place runs. The checker … refuses at the numeral's place a number that does not fit, for a coercion of the numeral's own component." The gated walk test is `tests/NumeralCoercionNumberRangeWalk.fss`, whose comment says "refused where the numeral's place runs". Its `.test` is `load_exception_contains=param 1 ($w:ZZ32) got arg 3000000000`. The binding is top level, so it runs during load.

**What is lost.** Before the update, "refused statically" stated a decided rule that no path built, and the deleted departure said what walk did. The deleted workaround also gave walk's timing: the getter raised at run time. Now the paragraph reads as the tree's behaviour on both paths ("So `Byte`'s body is `Byte(v)`" holds on both). But nothing says that walk refuses a number that does not fit only where the place runs, as a run-time error ('got arg'). So "refused statically" claims more than F-407 for walk. The same section gives this path difference for the two neighbouring cases:
- `:97`: "is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs".
- `:99`: "The checker refuses statically a numeral that breaks it … Walk refuses it when the binding runs."

**Consequence for a worker.** A worker writes a walk test that expects a refusal before the program runs, or no load exception at all. Or the worker takes a walk program that loads as proof that its coercion's numbers fit, although a place that has not yet run can still refuse. The fix is about six words, in `:97`'s form: "is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs."

Row 1131 adds a compiled limit: the static refusal covers only a coercion of the numeral's own component. The admission keeps that limit out of the text on purpose ("Placed elsewhere", below). This failure is walk's half only, which the admission did not weigh.

## Kept only in a destination that is owed a rewrite

### B: the departure for plain functional methods of a generic trait

**Old** (`:17`): "For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object at each call, not at load (row 780)." Its source, `sources.md:1274`, points to `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks".

**New** (`:17`): "For example, walk refuses a valid pair of generic functional methods of a generic trait, one inside the other, at an extending object's first instance (row 780)."

It survives in the destination that `:17` points to. `interpreter.md:64` says "Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type", and `:68` says "At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call …".

But `:68` is the line that the admission (item 3) and the writer (`writer-1.log`) list for rewriting as "false since rung G". **When `:68` is rewritten, change only its row 780 clause, so that the pair stops at an extending object's first instance.** Keep its first two sentences for plain functional methods, under P-45 and F-26, without row 780. Otherwise this departure, which P-45 still lists, leaves the skill.

## Placed elsewhere by the admission (checked, not failures)

- **A, row 1134.** F-26 and F-253 now give this exception to the rule at `:15`: "except two whose bounds differ only in the api of a type of one simple name, of which the object's is kept (row 1134)". The new `:15` does not carry it. The admission makes it a wall for the coordinator (P-180, `403a0e60cb`). `coordinator/PLAN.md:61` lists row 1134 for the batch after, so it is placed.

7	## 1. What I would do differently, section by section
8	
9	### Preamble (lines 1-7)
10	
11	- Read each bold sentence as the rule of this tree; a sentence with a P-N as a
12	  curator decision; a sentence with a row or an F-N as unsettled behaviour.
13	- For a row case that the rules decide, write an `XXX` test that asserts the

15	  behaviour and cite the row (or the F-N).
16	- Leave every limit that opens "Until the switch-over" alone in the compiler's
17	  prelude; it ends when the compiled path moves to the interpreter's library.
18	- Search FACTS and POSITIONS before calling a disagreement a conflict.
19	- Distrust old notes, team tests and my own training on three points: the
20	  number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, walk
21	  converts arguments.
22	- Limits: when sources disagree, the later type papers usually beat the early
23	  specification text (P-26). The original specification text sits in

26	### Dispatch and overloading (lines 9-24)
27	
28	- I may overload on static-parameter bounds alone
29	  (`ident[\T extends Shape\]` beside `ident[\T extends Round\]`), judged on
30	  declared domains. The more specific overload's return type must fit the
31	  other's at every instance the arguments allow, not just one (P-45).
32	- For generic overloads that rely on exclusion, I would tie the static
33	  parameters through a shared generic type at some position (`Box[\T\]` in
34	  both). If the exclusion needs a parameter that nothing ties, both paths
35	  refuse the pair (P-152). In the exclusion test the checker replaces a bare

43	  trait. When an object inherits an abstract functional method from one trait
44	  and its body from another, I would redeclare the method in the object
45	  (P-149), unlike Scala.

47	  add `excludes { Number }` (or `excludes { HasRank }` if the trait extends

# Cold read of the orientation (climb-batch-36)

Read: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md` (the core), and
`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-36/orientation/orientation.md`. Nothing
else was opened. Line numbers below are those of `orientation.md`.

## 1. What I would do differently, section by section

### Preamble (lines 1-7)

- Read each bold sentence as the rule of this tree; a sentence with a P-N as a
  curator decision; a sentence with a row or an F-N as unsettled behaviour.
- For a row case that the rules decide, write an `XXX` test that asserts the
  rule's answer. For one they do not decide, write a plain test of today's
  behaviour and cite the row (or the F-N).
- Leave every limit that opens "Until the switch-over" alone in the compiler's
  prelude; it ends when the compiled path moves to the interpreter's library.
- Search FACTS and POSITIONS before calling a disagreement a conflict.
- Distrust old notes, team tests and my own training on three points: the
  number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, walk
  converts arguments.
- Limits: when sources disagree, the later type papers usually beat the early
  specification text (P-26). The original specification text sits in
  `Specification-1.0-frozen/` (the Working Draft) and in Appendix I.

### Dispatch and overloading (lines 9-24)

- I may overload on static-parameter bounds alone
  (`ident[\T extends Shape\]` beside `ident[\T extends Round\]`), judged on
  declared domains. The more specific overload's return type must fit the
  other's at every instance the arguments allow, not just one (P-45).
- For generic overloads that rely on exclusion, I would tie the static
  parameters through a shared generic type at some position (`Box[\T\]` in
  both). If the exclusion needs a parameter that nothing ties, both paths
  refuse the pair (P-152). In the exclusion test the checker replaces a bare
  parameter by the meet of its bounds, but not one inside a static argument
  (P-157).
- I would never rely on declaration order under walk. I would not take walk's
  load check as a verdict in either direction; I would look the case up in
  `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks".
- I would not declare `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)`. I would not put
  an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one
  trait. When an object inherits an abstract functional method from one trait
  and its body from another, I would redeclare the method in the object
  (P-149), unlike Scala.
- For a program trait with its own functional `+`, `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` I would
  add `excludes { Number }` (or `excludes { HasRank }` if the trait extends
  `Number`), or declare the operator in an object. Otherwise walk refuses the
  program at load, and the checker does not warn me (row 918).

### Traits and objects (lines 26-64)

- I would never let a type extend two instantiations of one generic trait. Only
  the checker catches it. Under walk, overloads on `Tg[\3\]` and `Tg[\4\]` are
  refused (row 416). I would not copy spec examples marked "Not allowed".
- A `comprises` list need not name every subtype; several declarations can
  cover a meet together (P-60).
- I would use `override` only to widen. To replace an inherited method at the
  same parameter types, I would redeclare it without `override`. A Java-style
  `override` is an error on both paths, and in the library it stops every
  walk program.
- I would cover each inherited abstract method in an object with one body or
  several narrower ones (P-147). Walk does not check generic objects
  (row 665). The checker refuses a cover by several bodies when static
  parameters take part (row 725).
- Self-typed traits: in a body, `self` is `T[\X\]` ∩ `X`, so no cast is needed.
  For a `typecase` that returns `self` in one arm, I would bind
  `do r: X = self; r end` (row 1070). I would write a compiled test before
  relying on a call of an `X` method in a generic object that lists `T`
  first (row 1052). Where an object redeclares an abstract dotted method of
  `T`, I would keep `T`'s return type, or use getters for a method without
  parameters (row 1094).
- `Index`: in the library and in code checked against the one library I would
  write `I extends Index`. I would remember that only `ZZ32` is an `Index`,
  that a tuple of `Index` types is one, that `()` is not, and that the
  compiler's prelude has no `Index` yet.
- Ordering: I would compare tuples only when every element is a
  `StandardPartialOrder`. Under walk I would not mix numeric types at one
  position (row 511). I would not expect a `List[\RR64\]` to be ordered in the
  checker (P-154).
- Equality: where a type has no `=`, `=` is `SEQV` (P-168). So I would give
  every value object that holds strings or other reference objects its own
  `=`. I would not rely on `=` for tuples longer than three (row 923). I would
  not confuse `≣`/`SEQV`/`===` with `≡`/`EQV`, which is defined on booleans
  only.

### Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes (lines 66-85)

- A static parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not `Nothing`
  (P-48). Under walk it can be `OPEN` or `Bottom` in the three listed cases.
- Under walk I would write the static arguments of a generic call that is
  itself an argument (`mk[\ZZ64\]()`), since walk gives it no expected type
  (P-51, row 705).
- I would use only the three `where` forms (P-151). The checker silently
  treats any other `where` on an `extends` entry as unconditional. I would not
  count on any `where` being checked at run time, and I would keep calls that
  introduce `where [\nat n\]` out of compiled code (row 867).
- I would write sizes in one fixed order: `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0` (P-55).
  Size exponents stay at or below 4096 and are never negative.
- I would keep `NatReflect.reflect` out of compiled programs (row 307).

### Numbers (lines 87-116)

- I would never extend a number type; a program's own number type goes below
  `Number` (P-160). I would replace `Int`/`Long`/`Float`/`BigNum`/
  `UnsignedLong` with `ZZ32`/`ZZ64`/`RR64`/`ZZ`/`NN64`, and write a catch-all
  arm as `x: Any =>`.
- I would type a binding that should not get a numeral's default
  (`q: QQ = 0.1`, not `x = 0.1` then `q: QQ = x`). A numeral at `Any`,
  `Object`, `Number`, `Index` or an unbounded parameter takes its default.
- I would declare a program number type's numeral coercion generic over
  `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` with a `where` bound. I would add a `QQ`
  coercion if it should take folded quotients (P-174).
- In tests of run-time arithmetic or `||`, I would give one operand as a
  typed variable so that folding does not decide the result (P-173).
- Under walk I would not rely on conversion at a declared return type
  (row 387) or on arrow-type conversion of a function argument (row 1083).
- To convert between integer types I would use the `asZZ32`-style getters
  (they raise) or the low-bits functions (they wrap) (P-161). In the one
  library I would write `asFloat(x)`, not `x.asRR64` (F-324). I would write no
  arithmetic on a `T extends Number`.
- I would use `DIV` for integer division, `(1.0 s) / n` for a float quotient,
  and a float or `QQ` base for negative powers. A compiled `7 / 2` is a static
  error until the switch-over.

### Reductions and comprehensions (lines 118-130)

- I would write the static argument of `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`
  whenever the value lands at a method's return type, a field, a top-level
  variable or an assignment (row 1008). I would always write both arguments of
  `BIG MIN_MAX` (row 1007).
- For a reduction without an identity I would extend
  `AssociativeReduction[\R\]` and declare `simpleJoin` at `R`, not at `Any` or
  untyped as the team's tests do.

### Implementation limits (lines 132-136)

- I would never use a `Maybe` as an `if` condition.
- I would write every parameter type, even where walk tolerates a missing one.

## 2. Passages that would send a worker wrong, read two ways, or use a term the core does not give

Confidence is my estimate that a worker would be misled or confused.

1. **Line 57 vs line 64: "`SEQV` follows the specification on both paths"**
   (confidence 0.7). Line 64 then says that the compiler's `≣` compares
   strings and the four fixed-width/float types by `=` (row 908), so a string
   equals an equal string compiled, and `0.0`/`-0.0`/NaN behave differently.
   The compiler's library also has no `=` over `Any`. So line 64's
   "`V(s) = V(t)` is `false`" does not hold on the compiled path today. A
   worker writing a both-path equality test from the bullet list would assert
   wrongly. The bullets need "under the one library", or the row cited at
   line 57.

2. **Bold rules stated as a difference between paths, then a row on one side**
   (confidence 0.7). Line 74 says "**Only the checker gives … context (P-51)**"
   and then "(row 705)". Line 122 says "**the two paths fix an unwritten static
   argument from different places**" and line 124 cites row 1008. The preamble
   says a bold rule is the rule of the tree and a row marks a departure. Here
   the bold rule describes the departure itself, so a worker cannot tell
   whether to write an `XXX` test (the checker's answer is the rule) or a plain
   test of each path.

3. **Line 48: "in your own generic … that runs under walk or is checked against
   the interpreter's library, write `I extends Index`"** (confidence 0.6). The
   next sentences say that walk runs the code without the bound and that the
   compiler's prelude has no `Index`. A worker writing a test for both paths
   would add the bound because "runs under walk", and the compiled half would
   then fail. The bound is needed only where the code is checked against the
   one library. The passage does not say what a both-path program writes
   before the switch-over (presumably no bound).

4. **Line 5/7: what to cite for a bold rule without a P-N** (confidence 0.5).
   The preamble says "Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a
   decision". The core's citable sources are the brief, a record entry or a
   primary source, and the skill is none of them. Many rules carry neither a
   P-N nor a row (`override` widens, `/` gives `QQ`, tuple ordering, "Write
   every parameter type"). A worker does not know whether to cite the
   orientation, reproduce the behaviour, or look up a FACTS entry.

5. **Line 91: a tuple arm with an undefined name** (confidence 0.55). It reads
   as a binder "on both paths" that "takes any element". Yet "Compiled, with an
   `Any` selector, the checker refuses that arm: … unreachable." The two
   statements seem to contradict each other. It is unclear whether row 1064's
   departure (binder reading) holds in the checker at all, and why the arm is
   unreachable.

6. **Line 64: row 923** (confidence 0.5). The sentence is "`(s, 1, 2, 3) =
   (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false` (row 923)". By the bold
   rule (no `=` declared → `SEQV`), `false` is the rule's answer, so it is
   unclear what departs. Is the missing `=` on 4-tuples the departure? A
   worker cannot tell whether to assert `true` in an `XXX` test or `false` in a
   plain test.

7. **Line 17: "at an extending object's first instance (row 780)"**
   (confidence 0.5). "First instance" is undefined. It could be the first
   instantiation of a generic object, the first object constructed, or the
   first `extends` entry. "One inside the other" presumably means one domain
   inside the other.

8. **Line 122: "A reduction whose bound does not name its parameter takes its
   bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit."**
   (confidence 0.45). "Fit" has no stated object. It could mean the bound
   does not fit the expected type or the body's type, or that the reduction
   cannot be instantiated at its bound.

9. **"Until the switch-over" marker missing or inconsistent** (confidence 0.4).
   Line 89, "The compiler's prelude declares no `QQ`", is a limit of the
   compiler's library but lacks the marker. Read by the preamble's rule, it is
   neither protected from a prelude fix nor clearly temporary. Lines 7, 64 and
   114 say "compiler's library" while the preamble's prohibition names the
   "compiler's prelude". The core says the prelude is three files of that
   library, so a worker may wonder whether a limit in a non-prelude file of
   the compiler's library may be fixed.

10. **Line 68: `OPEN`** (confidence 0.4). "Every value passes `OPEN` itself"
    is followed by "a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at
    `Bottom`". The difference between the whole type and a type that holds
    `OPEN` is easy to miss. The rule's own answer for `pick((1, 2))` is not
    given, so row 663 cannot become an `XXX` test.

11. **Line 30: "as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`"** (confidence 0.4). The
    example does not say which trait declares the `comprises` clause or what
    it lists, so the reader cannot check the claim it illustrates.

12. **Line 38: "a `comprises` clause … that lists only `...`"**
    (confidence 0.4). `comprises { ... }` is not given by the core, and its
    meaning (a hidden list in an api?) is not explained.

13. **Rows whose rule answer is not stated** (confidence 0.35). A worker needs
    the rule's answer to write the `XXX` test the preamble asks for. It is not
    given for:
    - line 55, row 511, `(1,2) < (1,2.5)`: true by promotion?
    - line 97, row 962, nat parameter ≥ 2^31: is walk's `ZZ64` the departure,
      or the compiled error, or both?
    - line 126, row 716, empty `SUM` without a declared type;
    - line 136, row 405: what walk does in "a method that implements an
      abstract one".

14. **Line 41: row 1052** (confidence 0.35). "No test covers such a body" is a
    coverage gap. It is neither a departure nor an undecided case, the two
    meanings the preamble gives a row. "Lists `T` first" implies that the
    order of `extends` entries matters on the compiled path, and nowhere else
    is this said.

15. **Line 85: "Such a call runs only under walk, also after the switch-over"**
    (confidence 0.35). This is a permanent claim, but the reason given is
    row 307, a departure that "can change" by the preamble's own terms.

16. **Line 15: "Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes"**
    (confidence 0.35). It is vague: instances of which declarations, compared
    by what?

17. **Line 81 ("emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check
    it") and line 134 (walk accepts a `Maybe` condition)** (confidence 0.3).
    Both describe a gap from the rule but cite no row. By the preamble they
    would be settled behaviour.

18. **Line 99: coercion timing** (confidence 0.3). "the compiled path when the
    class loads, before `run()`" leaves out the consequence. A coercion that
    raises (or prints) would do so before the program starts, outside any
    `try` in the program. If that is the point, it should say so.

19. **Line 110: "`big` … keep[s] the low bits"** (confidence 0.3). For an
    `NN64` with its top bit set, it is unclear whether `big` gives the
    unsigned value or a negative `ZZ`.

20. **Line 32: "a generic self-typed trait"** (confidence 0.3). It is used
    before "self-typed" is defined at line 36.

21. **Line 19: "So the checker refuses …"** (confidence 0.3). The duplicate
    case where `self` stands at different positions names only the checker,
    while the two bullets below say "both paths". It is unclear whether walk
    refuses the first case.

22. **Terms not given by the core** (confidence 0.25-0.3 each):
    - "nest" (line 24, for "one strictly more specific");
    - "meet" of bounds (line 13);
    - "extenders" (line 30);
    - `0#n` range syntax (line 120);
    - "the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators" (line 101). The
      preamble promises "fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap", but no
      section names the wrapping operators;
    - `Unordered` (line 55);
    - "Appendix I keeps the original text" (line 5): of which document,
      `Specification/` or the frozen draft?
    - the references are cited without their `references/` prefix
      (`compiler.md`, `interpreter.md`). This is minor.

23. **Placement** (confidence 0.2). Tuple ordering and `SEQV` (lines 55-64)
    sit under "Traits and objects". A worker looking for equality or ordering
    would look under "Numbers" or for a section of their own.

## 3. Repair history, or detail that changes no action and prevents no misunderstanding

1. **Line 41: "runs, also from an arm of a conditional or a `case`
   expression, a function expression or a local function."** This reads as a
   list of shapes that were fixed one by one. The action needs only the one
   failing shape, the `typecase` (row 1070). Medium.
2. **Line 43: "With the reading of the exclusion test and the bounds that the
   test reads …, the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a
   number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own."** This justifies why the
   library passes. A worker takes no action on it, unless the point is "do
   not 'fix' this pair", which the sentence does not say. Low-medium.
3. **Line 17: the row 780 example.** The action is to look the case up in
   `interpreter.md`, and the example adds nothing to that. It is also unclear
   (item 2.7). Low-medium.
4. **Line 134: "Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over
   (P-12)."** This is a future plan. "Walk has no static types" repeats the
   core ("The tree has no static types"). The section's actionable content is
   the `Maybe` condition. Low-medium.
5. **Line 15: "It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the
   arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function."** This reads like
   the announcement of a fix. No action follows unless a worker expected
   otherwise. Low.
6. **Line 43: "There the intersection is the object's own type, so the two
   declarations have one domain"**. This explains the mechanism of row 1094.
   The action ("Declare the object's method at `T`'s return type") stands
   without it. Low; it may help a worker who fixes row 1094.
7. **Line 99: "walk computes it at the place's first run, the compiled path
   when the class loads, before `run()`"**. This is implementation detail with
   no stated action (see item 2.18). Keep it only if the consequence is
   written. Low.

Kept, though borderline:
- "The record calls the number types 'the tower'" (line 89): it prevents
  misreading the record.
- The quoted error messages (lines 89, 95, 124): they let a worker recognise
  the case.
- "The Scala language accepts it" (line 22) and "A Java `permits` list names
  each direct subtype" (line 30): they prevent the expected
  misunderstanding.

1	# Quiz grading, round 1 (cases 3, 18 and 32)

The key: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/regression/key.md`, cases 3, 18 and 32, as climb batch 36's update reads them (the working tree on `main` at `906bbb4607`, with the update not yet committed). The orientation graded: `orientation.md` in this folder. Each case is graded on its decision and scope, by the key's **Expected**, **Scope**, **Wrong** and **Partial** lists.

8	- Right without its path or scope qualification: 0.

17	- The validity argument is on declared domains: `Box[\Circle\]` lies strictly inside the generic's domain, so no meet is needed; both return `String`, at every instance; the domains are not equal, so No Duplicates holds.

19	- Scope matches the key's **Scope**:
20	  - Walk loads the pair: a generic beside a plain declaration, checked on declared domains.
21	  - The compiled checker accepts it (P-45), checked today through the count or distance stage.
22	  - The reader adds that compiled programs do not link the interpreter's library before the switch-over, except with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. This is true and narrows nothing the key needs.
23	- None of the key's **Wrong** answers appears: no refusal, renaming or merging, no conflict, no reordering, and the generic does not run for `Box[\Circle\]`.

The reader reads row 416 rightly: walk applies no instantiation exclusion, so it refuses an overload on two instantiations of one generic type.

The task is a library task, the walk fix is in another area, so the reader follows the library's own way in `RangeInternals.fss`, a name of its own for the new declaration. This is the key's "distinct names by rank". The reader puts the walk fix, starting from row 416's reproducer, to the curator as a decision not taken, and notes row 416 in the ledger if the brief allows, else in the report. The key's **Open** accepts either repair.
31	- Scope matches the key's **Scope**: both declarations plain, both positions instances of one generic type, and walk refusing with "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The compiled checker accepts the pair; compiled programs before the switch-over do not link `RangeInternals`.
32	- None of the key's **Wrong** answers appears:
33	  - No reordering, no pair called invalid, no new ledger row, no edit of the compiler's prelude.
34	  - The stop is not matched to row 780, the example that the orientation's rule on walk's load check now gives. The reader quotes the orientation's rule on the exclusion rule, with its `Tg[\3\]` and `Tg[\4\]` example and row 416, not row 780's generic functional methods.

38	- The declaration is the key's:
39	
40	      value object Byte(b: ZZ32) extends Number
41	          coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v)
42	      end
43	
44	  - The body is `Byte(v)`, and `v` converts where it stands, at `Byte`'s `ZZ32` parameter. The reader says that `x: Byte = 255` binds `Byte(255)` on both paths. The reader names no departure, and writes no getter, helper or `XXX` test of the rule. So the reader avoids the key's new **Wrong** item and the old `Byte(v.asZZ32)`.
45	  - `extends Number` is the key's declaration plus P-160's placement. The orientation says that such a type runs on both paths (`orientation.md:89`), and `Number` declares nothing (P-165), so it changes no answer.

47	  - Compiled, before and after the switch-over: refused statically, with the key's message, 'The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte.' The program never runs.
48	  - Walk: refused when the binding runs. At the top level, while the top-level variables are initialised, which the harness counts as a refusal at load; inside `run()`, when execution reaches the binding. This is the key's split. The reader does not quote walk's messages and would take them from a run; the key does not require them.
49	- `z: Byte = 2 + 3`: does not bind. The reader gives the key's reason: the expression folds before the checker into the constant 5 at its default `ZZ32`, a program's own type takes it only through a coercion from that type, and coercions do not chain. It is refused statically compiled and at the binding's run under walk.

**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".

**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk refuses a valid pair of generic functional methods of a generic trait, one inside the other, at an extending object's first instance (row 780).
Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value, other than a numeral type's number, is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).
Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A program's own number type takes a numeral through a coercion generic over its numbers, which its body declares, as `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 }`. With a radix point, write `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])`. The static arguments of either form are naturals of any size. In the body, each converts where it stands, into the type that its place fixes. A numeral whose number does not fit there is refused statically. It is a `ZZ` only where nothing fixes a type (P-174, P-173, P-40). So `Byte`'s body is `Byte(v)`. The `where` clause bounds the numerals that the type takes. The checker refuses statically a numeral that breaks it, as `300` here: 'The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte.' Walk refuses it when the binding runs. A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches the type as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written: walk computes it at the place's first run, the compiled path when the class loads, before `run()` (`compiler.md`, "What the code generator does"). Each run of that place reuses it (P-176). Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.

+
+This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. Where the rules decide the case, assert their answer in an `XXX` test. Where they do not, assert today's behaviour in a plain test, one without the `XXX` prefix, and cite the row (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded"). A departure that cites a FACTS entry (F-N) in place of a row is known too: test it as one that cites a row, and cite the entry. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.

A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance that the argument types allow, not at one only.
+
+**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value has at most one instance of a given generic type. So where both declarations name the same generic type at a position, a value of both domains makes the two static arguments equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair whose exclusion needs a static parameter that the equalities leave free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
+

Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".

Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk refuses a valid pair of generic functional methods of a generic trait, one inside the other, at an extending object's first instance (row 780).
+

+- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
+- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.

So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. The interpreter's library declares it and its negation `≢` (`NEQV`) for booleans only, so on other values each is a type error. The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:

+- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
+- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
+- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.

The interpreter's library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false` (row 923). To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its `≣`, declared as `===` over `Any`, follows `SEQV` but compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).

+## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes
+
+**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: in a generic object whose `T` stayed open, a call `pick((1, 2))` of its methods `pick(x: Any)` and `pick(x: (T,T))` runs the first (row 663). Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
+
+- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
+- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
+- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
+
+**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
+
+**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
+
+- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
+- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
+
+The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension without its condition (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
+
+**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).

+**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call runs only under walk, also after the switch-over. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, which lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.
